content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies the problem of Pareto frontier approximation via scalarization in multi-objective stochastic linear bandits. In this paper, the authors first extend the standard Bayes regret to the scalarized Bayes regret in the multi-objective setting, which has a close relation to hypervolume regret via the hypervolume scalarization technique. Then they design a UCB algorithm based on random scalarization, showing convergence to the Pareto frontier. This paper further instantiates the scalarization in the proposed method to be hypervolume scalarization, and provides an upper bound as well as a lower bound for the hypervolume regret. The simulation experiment compares various scalarization methods, indicating the superiority of hypervolume scalarization over other methods empirically.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

+ This paper provides sufficient and very detailed background knowledge of scalarization methods in multi-objective optimization.
+ The lower bound for the hypervolume regret in multi-objective bandits is novel and interesting.


Weaknesses:

- Some statements in this paper are not well-supported and seem overclaimed.
(i) Although it is titled “provable multi-objective optimization”, this paper only examines the setting of multi-objective stochastic linear bandits, without further explanation on how the proposed algorithm/analysis can be extended to more general multi-objective optimization scenarios. 
(ii) I am not fully understand how the optimal scalarization method is suggested by the analysis in this paper, since the performance metric (i.e., the regret) is defined specific to the given (random) scalarization method $s_\lambda$. In particular, with different choices of scalarization functions, the Bayes regret itself varies, so directly comparing their respective regret bounds might be unfair. It would be helpful to add some remarks and explanations on the main theorem.

- In the contribution and experiment parts, it is claimed that hypervolume scalarization is more suitable to RL. However, there seems no theoretical or empirical evidence on this point. In particular, the experiment is conducted on a simulated bandits setup, which I think is different from the RL setup. In addition, I am not sure if the empirical comparison of different scalarization methods is fair, since the performance metric, i.e., the hypervolume regret, is the special case of the proposed scalarized regret based on hypervolume scalarization. 

- This paper has an overlap with previous works on the hypervolume scalarization, which should be compared in more detail. For example, this paper comments that (Paria et al 2018) is unclear how to choose the right scalarization, but the optimal scalarization seems also unclear in this paper (see the first weakness). Moreover, since random hypervolume scalarization is also investigated in (Golovin and Zhang 2020), it would be better to compare the proposed random scalarization algorithm and the technical detail with Golovin’s work (for example, how the constant $k$ in the regret bound is saved). 

- The presentation of this paper seems very messy.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Some part of this paper is well-written and easy to follow. But some other parts are quite messy, without a clear logic flow. 

The analysis seems technically sound and the lower bound provided for hypervolume regret is novel. However, some statements (e.g., how to choose optimal scalarization) are not well supported and a bit overclaimed, and the comparison with previous works is not sufficient (especially on hypervolume scalarization). Thus, the novelty seems to be lowered.

Please see the Weaknesses part for more details.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper contributes a scalarized Bayes regret metric and a UCB-based random scalarization algorithm for multi-objective stochastic linear bandits. The analysis is general and the lower bound for hypervolume regret is interesting and novel. However, it is not clear how the theoretical and empirical results would suggest the optimal choice of scalarization since the regret metric is specific to the certain choice of scalarization and not aligned. In addition, this paper seems to have a strong overlap with previous works on hypervolume scalarization, which need to be carefully compared.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose and algorithm that minimizes hyper-volume regret via a novel non-Euclidean analysis and metric entropy. They establish a tight lower bound on both the hyper-volume regret and the Bayes regret by introducing a packing argument on the Pareto set. They have empirical results for their algorithm to show that they do indeed find a higher hyper-volume.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper proposes a novel algorithm for discovering the Pareto optimal frontier by maximizing the hyper volume. This is an interesting problem and they show both theoretical and empirical results.

The paper relies on a two step procedure of selecting a secalarizing vector and then finding the best arm by using UCB for the collapsed single objective linear bandit algorithm using UCB. It is not clear why UCB is used. There are other more optimized linear bandit algorithms for linear contextual bandits. A lot of the analysis uses pre-existing results for UCB and therefore the contributions of this paper are only marginally better.

The paper would be made stronger if they could compare to an existing algorithm such as IMO^3 and see how this work compares to them. It would also have been good to compare against the following straw man: randomly choose scalarizing vectors and then solve a linear contextual bandit for each.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clear in its exposition and it reads clearly. One issue is that the lemma used in the algorithm is in the appendix which make it hard to read since you have to go back and forth.
content.summary_of_the_review: This is an interesting paper on a topic of interest but comparing to another algorithm like IMO^3 would have made it stronger.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper considers the problem of multi-objective stochastic linear bandits. For this problem, they define the notion of hypervolume regret. They design an UCB based algorithm that achieves a regret upper-bound on this hypervolume regret and prove a corresponding lower-bound for any algorithm. The motivation of this paper is to study the optimal weights on any linearization method of the multiple objectives into a single scalar quantity.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths

+ The topic of study is important and foundational understanding of multi-objective bandits is important. Thus, providing new definitions and algorithms (e.g., hypervolume regret) is an important step forward.

+ The paper is overall well-written and accessible. 

Weakness

- Overall I felt the paper to be a bit lacking in explaining the main significance. First, it is not directly clear why hyper-volume regret is significant. They motivate this via the fact that maximizing the hyper-volume of the pareto set is considered to be a widely accepted notion since it can provide a diverse set of pareto points in the offline maximization problem. But, can the authors give a much more stronger explanation for the bandit setting? May be an example where a bandit algorithm needs to identify a diverse set of pareto points? I find the result on converging to a a given scalarized function as a function of the lipshitz constant to be meaningful. I generally think the paper needs to go a bit deeper on the hypervolume regret and why multi-objective linear bandit needs to optimize this metric is better than other scalarizations, since that is the main contribution.

- To substantiate the above, in my opinion, the algorithm itself isn't novel. Its using linUCB and combining each step with the scalarized function. I also suspect that one does not need to use linUCB per-se, but any algorithm that maximizes a single objective for the linear bandit problem can be used as a blackbox. Most of the heavylifting is done in step 6. Is this true? If so,
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity

- The paper presents their main ideas and the contributions clearly. The theory and the experiments are clear and identify the main point. 

Quality

- Overall the considered problem is significant and the research is of good quality. The main theorems are correct to the best of my reading. The authors have all the important quantities in the main theorem.

Novelty

- Overall, I find this paper to me mostly conceptual. Although the authors claim the algorithm is new, I personally thing the algorithm is not novel. The algorithm should be used as a template to elucidate the main conceptual points.

Reproducibility

- To the most part, the main results of this paper can be reproduced.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I am supportive of the direction this paper considers. I believe that foundational understanding of different scalarizations in the context of multi-objective linear bandits is important. However, I have some concerns around the motivation of the exact definition in this paper in the context of linear bandits. In particular, although it seems natural extension from the offline setting, I want the authors to put in more thought on potential applications and explain the results through the lens of this application. Moreover, I would also encourage the authors to think if the main results really depend on using linUCB vs any algorithm for linear bandits (this will also make the notion of hypervolume regret more stronger).

content.title: Optimal Scalarizations for Provable Multiobjective Optimization
content.TL;DR: Don't linearly combine your objectives: Hypervolume scalarizations provide provable and more optimal multiobjective optimization.
content.abstract: Linear scalarization is a simple and widely-used technique that can be deployed in any multiobjective setting to combine diverse objectives into one reward function, but such heuristics are not theoretically understood. To that end, we perform a case study of the multiobjective stochastic linear bandits framework with $k$ objectives and our goal is to provably scalarize and explore a diverse set of optimal actions on the Pareto frontier, as measured by the dominated hypervolume. Even in this elementary convex setting, the choice of scalarizations and weight distribution surprisingly affects performance, and the natural use of linear scalarization with uniform weights is suboptimal due to a non-uniform Pareto curvature. Instead, we suggest the usage of the theoretically-inspired hypervolume scalarizations with non-adaptive uniform weights, showing that it comes with novel hypervolume regret bounds of  $\tilde{O}( d T^{-1/2} + T^{-1/k})$, with optimal matching lower bounds of $\Omega(T^{-1/k})$. We support our theory with strong empirical performance of the hypervolume scalarization that consistently outperforms both the linear and Chebyshev scalarizations in high dimensions.
